how-much-should-i-charge-for-an-interpre.text:
← Back to the sign language interpreter rate calculator

How much should a sign language interpreter charge for an assignment?

Start from your own hourly rate, then apply the conventions that actually move the number: a booking minimum, a team-interpreting surcharge on long high-stakes work, and a late-cancellation fee schedule. The rest of this page works through each on real numbers, not rounded examples.

The booking minimum changes a short request

A 1.5-hour request at $65/hour, standard business hours, one interpreter:

FigureArithmeticResult
Raw hourly math (what it looks like at a glance)1.5 hrs × $65$97.50
Billable hours under a 2-hour minimummax(1.5, 2)2 hrs
Actual interpreting fee2 hrs × $65$130.00

A $32.50 gap between the number a quick mental calculation gives and the number the commonly cited freelance booking minimum actually bills -- the interpreter has reserved two hours of unsellable time, not 90 minutes.

A team-interpreting assignment doubles the fee, not the rate

A 3-hour legal deposition at $65/hour -- past the length and in a setting RID's own guidance names for team-interpreting consideration:

StaffingArithmeticTotal
Single interpreter3 hrs × $65$195.00
Two-interpreter team$195.00 × 2$390.00

Both interpreters bill the same three-hour block, so the fee reflects two professionals working the assignment, not a higher hourly rate for one. This calculator flags the recommendation on a booking like this rather than pricing it automatically -- the actual staffing decision depends on the venue, the funder, and the interpreters involved.

A late cancellation is not automatically the full fee

A $200.00 scheduled booking, cancelled with two different amounts of notice, under a commonly cited three-tier schedule (full fee inside 24 hours, half fee 24-48 hours, no fee beyond 48 hours):

Notice givenTierFee owed
18 hoursUnder 24 hours notice$200.00 (100%)
30 hours24-47.9 hours notice$100.00 (50%)

A twelve-hour difference in notice given is a $100.00 difference in what is owed -- the schedule rewards earlier notice without waiving the fee outright.

Do this with your own assignment

The sign language interpreter rate calculator runs this same arithmetic on your own hours, rate, setting, differential, travel, and cancellation notice. Nothing you type leaves your browser.

Common questions

How much should a freelance sign language interpreter charge for an assignment?

Start from your own hourly rate, then apply the conventions that actually move the number. A 1.5-hour request at $65/hour is not a $97.50 invoice -- the commonly cited two-hour freelance booking minimum applies, so the assignment bills as 2 hours at $65 for a $130.00 total, a $32.50 difference the raw hourly math never shows.

Why does a two-hour minimum matter if the assignment is shorter?

A freelance interpreter who accepts a 45-minute booking has turned away any other work that could have filled that same block, including the travel time on either side of it. A minimum-booking policy is the industry's commonly cited answer to that: the interpreter is paid for the time reserved, not only the time actually interpreting.

How much does staffing a team of two interpreters actually add?

It doubles the interpreting fee, because both interpreters are billing the same block. A 3-hour legal assignment at $65/hour prices at $195.00 for a single interpreter; the same booking staffed as a recommended two-interpreter team prices at $390.00 -- the fee reflects two professionals working the assignment, not one at a higher rate.

No warranty. This page and the calculator it links to are not legal, medical, or financial advice, and they do not replace a qualified professional. Figures here are starting points from commonly cited industry conventions, not a quote, guarantee, or valuation performed on your behalf. Verify every figure against your own contract and negotiate your own assignment terms. Common questions

How much should a freelance sign language interpreter charge for an assignment?

Start from your own hourly rate, then apply the conventions that actually move the number: a commonly cited two-hour minimum for a freelance or contract booking, portal-to-portal travel time and mileage, and an after-hours, weekend, or holiday differential if the booking falls outside standard business hours. This calculator applies all four to your own numbers and returns a total, never a fixed quote.

Why does a two-hour minimum matter if the assignment is shorter?

A freelance interpreter who accepts a 45-minute booking has turned away any other work that could have filled that same block, including the travel time on either side of it. A minimum-booking policy is the industry's commonly cited answer to that: the interpreter is paid for the time reserved, not only the time actually interpreting.

When should an assignment be staffed with two interpreters instead of one?

RID's own Standard Practice Papers recommend a team of two interpreters, splitting turns roughly every 20-30 minutes, for assignments running past about two hours or carrying high cognitive load — legal, medical, and mental-health settings are the ones most often named. Sign language interpreting is simultaneous, bidirectional cognitive work with no natural pause, and interpreter fatigue on a long, high-stakes assignment measurably increases errors. This calculator flags the recommendation rather than pricing it automatically, because the actual decision depends on the specific venue, funder, and interpreters involved.

Is a late-cancellation fee normal, and how is it usually calculated?

Yes — a freelance interpreting contract commonly carries a tiered cancellation schedule, because a cancelled booking is unsold time the interpreter already turned other work away for. A commonly cited starting shape charges the full scheduled fee inside 24 hours' notice, half the fee between 24 and 48 hours, and nothing beyond 48 hours — adjustable here to match your own contract.

vs-a-flat-fee-per-assignment.html.text:
← back to the calculator

This calculator vs. a flat fee per assignment

A flat fee per assignment — one memorized number, quoted for most bookings — is the fastest way to answer "what do you charge?" on the phone. It stops working the moment a booking's travel, timing, or staffing needs differ from whatever booking the number was built around, because none of that is tracked separately in a single figure.

What each one is for

A flat fee per assignment is quick to quote and easy for a client to hear. What it does not do is separate the price into anything an interpreter can check against a specific booking — it does not add travel and mileage for a booking that is further away, it does not apply an after-hours differential to an evening or weekend request, and it cannot flag the one thing RID's own guidance says to check on a long, high-stakes booking: whether it should be staffed with a team.

This calculator bills the greater of hours requested or your booking minimum, adds portal-to-portal travel time and mileage, applies an evening/weekend or holiday differential, and flags — never auto-prices — a two-interpreter team recommendation on assignments RID's Standard Practice Papers name as long or high-stakes enough to need one.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What do I charge for a routine, nearby, standard-hours booking?Either one — a flat fee is fine if travel, timing, and setting rarely change.
What does travel and mileage actually add to this booking?This calculator — a flat number does not know how far today's assignment is.
Does this evening or weekend request change what I should charge?This calculator's differential, not a flat fee — a memorized number does not know what day it is.
Should this legal, medical, or mental-health booking be a team?This calculator's team-interpreting finding, computed from RID's own guidance, not a flat fee — a lump sum tracks no staffing at all.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?No. The calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent to a server.

Three bookings a flat fee prices the same way

All three start from the same $65/hour rate. A flat fee built around a typical booking prices all three identically; this calculator does not.

BookingA flat per-booking feeThis calculatorGap
1 hour, 20-minute travel each way, 10 miles round trip$130.00 (2-hour minimum, no travel)$180.03 (minimum + travel time + mileage)$50.03 in unbilled travel and mileage
3-hour booking, Saturday evening$195.00 (standard-hours rate)$292.50 (evening/weekend ×1.5)$97.50 missed differential
3-hour legal deposition, team recommended$195.00 (single-interpreter rate)$390.00 (two-interpreter team)$195.00 — one interpreter priced for work RID's guidance says two should share

The flat fee is not wrong on any one of these by design — it is the same number every time, and only one of these three bookings happens to match whatever assignment it was originally sized around. The other two are quietly under-quoted by the exact thing a single memorized figure cannot see.

Common questions

What is a flat fee per assignment, and why do interpreters use it?

One number an interpreter has memorized and quotes for most bookings — often built around their usual hourly rate and the commonly cited two-hour minimum. It is fast to say on the phone or in a text and easy for a client to hear, which is why many freelancers default to it for a routine-looking booking.

What does a flat fee miss on a short booking?

Travel. A flat number sized around the two-hour minimum can look right for a nearby booking and still leave real portal-to-portal drive time and mileage uncharged the moment the assignment is further away — a memorized number does not know how far today's booking is.

What does a flat fee miss on an evening or weekend booking?

The after-hours differential. A flat fee built around a standard-hours rate does not distinguish a weekday afternoon from a Saturday evening, so it quietly under-quotes the booking that is actually costing the interpreter their weekend.

Can a flat fee tell me when a booking needs a second interpreter?

No. A flat fee is a price, not a staffing check. Whether a long legal, medical, or mental-health assignment should be staffed with a two-interpreter team depends on the setting and length, per RID's own Standard Practice Paper guidance — a memorized number has no way to flag that, and quoting it as-is prices one interpreter for work the field's own guidance says two should share.

Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?

No. The calculator this page links to runs entirely in your browser; nothing you enter is uploaded.

vs-a-spreadsheet.html.text:
← Sign language interpreter rate calculator

This calculator vs. a spreadsheet

A lot of freelance interpreters already track fees in a spreadsheet: one column for hours, one for rate, a formula that multiplies them. That arithmetic is trivial and a spreadsheet does it fine once you already know the billable hours and the right multiplier. What it does not do on its own is apply the booking minimum, the after-hours differential, and portal-to-portal travel together -- three formulas to write and keep in sync, before you even get to the team-interpreting question a spreadsheet has no way to ask.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What's hours times a rate? Either one — a spreadsheet multiplies fine.
Should this booking bill the 2-hour minimum instead of the hours requested? This calculator — it bills the greater of the two automatically; a spreadsheet needs an IF formula you write and remember to apply.
Does an evening, weekend, or holiday differential apply, and by how much? This calculator — you pick it from a dropdown and the multiplier is derived, so it can't drift from what you picked.
Should this booking be staffed with two interpreters? This calculator — checks the setting and billable hours against RID's own Standard Practice Paper guidance and flags it; a spreadsheet has no way to ask this on its own.
What does travel time and mileage add, billed as their own fraction of the rate? This calculator — separate travel-time and mileage line items, computed from the minutes and miles you enter.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere? No, on either — but this calculator needs no template, no formula to maintain, and nothing to keep in sync across cells.
Calculate an assignment fee now

This tool needs no account and nothing installed: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and the hours, rate, setting, and travel details you enter stay on this device — nothing is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

Isn't an interpreting fee just hours times a rate?

The multiplication itself is trivial and a spreadsheet does it fine once you already know the billable hours and the right multiplier. What a plain spreadsheet does not do on its own is apply the booking minimum (billing the greater of hours requested or the minimum, not just the hours typed in), the after-hours/weekend/holiday differential, and portal-to-portal travel together — each is its own formula to write and keep in sync with the others.

Will a spreadsheet tell me when a booking should be staffed with two interpreters?

No. That is a judgment call from RID's own Standard Practice Papers, not an arithmetic rule a spreadsheet formula can express on its own unless you build and maintain a lookup by setting and length. This calculator checks the booking's setting and billable hours against that guidance automatically and surfaces it as a finding — it never forces the team rate on, but it also never lets a six-hour legal deposition go quietly priced for one interpreter.

What happens if I apply the wrong differential multiplier in my own sheet?

Nothing catches it — a spreadsheet returns whatever the formula says, whether the 1.5x evening/weekend or 2x holiday multiplier you typed matches the booking you actually have or not. This calculator derives the multiplier from the dropdown you select, so it can't drift from what you picked, and it separately reports the booking minimum, the differential, travel, and mileage as their own line items rather than one collapsed number.

Does this replace an interpreter's own income-tracking spreadsheet?

No. A spreadsheet or ledger that tracks every booking, every invoice, and every month's total over a year is still the right tool for that ongoing record. This page answers one question at a time — what should this one assignment cost, and does its setting and length suggest a team — and nothing it computes is saved anywhere once you leave the page.
